full_judgment:
D. C. Bhattachaiya, J.—Certain important questions having a bearing noun the construction and scope Of section 144 of the Code of Criminal Procedure Code have been raised in this petition under Article 102 of the Constitution. 

 2. On the 26th April, 1974 the Additional District Magistrate, Dacca issued an order under section 144 Criminal Procedure. Code prohibiting the holding of any public meeting, demonstrations, rallies and Processions in the City of Dacca and Narayanganj until further orders, with effect from 2 P. M on 26-4-74. The life of tins order was, according to clause (6) of section 144 of the Code, two months and on the 25th of June, 1974 another order under the aforesaid section was promulgated containing the same prohibitory directions, whit effect from 6 AM of the 26th of June, 1974 which was also to be in force until further orders. 

 3. The petitioner has described himself as a member of the Executive Committee of "Sharbadaliya Oikya Front", i.e, All Patties United Front and it has been alleged in the petition that the petitioner and other members of the said Front decided to hold a public meeting on the 30th June, 1974 at 4 P.M at Palten Maidan with a view to ventilating their political views peacefully in a democratic way in the exercise of their fundamental rights as guaranteed by the Constitution under the idea that the earlier prohibitory order would come to an end by the time they would be holding the said meeting but the Additional District vlagistrate, Dacca has issued a fresh order in the same terms in colorable exercise of his jurisdiction under section 144 Cr. P. Code for an indetinite period. This action of the Additional Distrito Magistrate has been assailed as male fide and it has been asserted that such an action his been taken in order to prevent the petitioner's Organization Islam holding the public meeting which has been widely published throughout the Country. 

 4. Dr. Aleem-al-Razee, the eared Advocate for the petitioner has mainly contended that the impugned order being a submissive order purported to be passed under section 144 of the Code of Criminal Procedure was beyond the competence of the Additional District Magistrate. It has also been argued by the learned Advocate that there having been no causal relationship between the acts Prohibited and the danger apprehended the order was beyond the score of section 144 Cr.P.C. and that the impugned order cannot be regarded as reasonable restriction within the meaning of Article 17 of the Constitution. The learned Advocate has also raised the question of constitutionality of section 144 Cr.P.C although in a half-hearted manner. 

 6. It should be noticed that section 144 Cr.P.C. by its very terms, is limited to an urgent case of apprehended danger and the order to he passed under it must be of limited duration. Before the constitutional guarantees were provided against any executive or legislative invasion upon the rights of the citizens which have been declared to be fundamental rights in the Constitution the question as to the scope and ambit of section 144 Cr. P. C. had come up for Judicial determination in variants Courts of the Indian sub-continent. There has been a consistency in judicial views that the powers granted under the said section being in derogation of the ordinary civil rights of the citizens, the provisions of the said section should be strictly construed and the power shall be sparingly used in cases of emergency only when there is no alternative to remedy for combating the apprehended danger. 

 8. The first two contentions of the learned Advocate for the petitioner are based on the nature and scope of the provisions of section 144 Cr.P.C. on the basis of the interpretation of the said provisions. 

 9. It has been contended by the learned Advocate for the petitioner that the provisions of section 144 Cr.P.C. is meant to be an emergency provision of an extremely temporary nature and that clause (6) of the said section having specifically provided that such an order shall not remain in for more than two months, the impugned order being nothing more than a continuation of the first order was without jurisdiction. 

 11. The earliest case in which the nature of a prohibitory order made under section 518 of Act X of 1872, which was the earlier version of section 144 of the Code of 1898, came up for consideration in the Full Bench case of Gopi Mohun Mullick Vs. Taramoni Chowdhury I.L.R. 5 Cal. 7 decided by a Bench of twelve Judges in 1879 and Chief Justice Garth in delivering the Judgment of the Full Bench observed that it was applicable only where a speedy remedy was called for and where a more formal procedure would be inappropriate. The learned Chief Justice proceeded to observe further; 

 13. The Patna High Court in the case of Rashbehari Singh and others Vs. Jagnarain Roy, A.I.R. 1917 Pat. 154 had to deal with a successive order under section 144 Cr.P.C. passed more than one month after the expiry of the first order and expressed their view in respect of the said order in the following words: 

 "We view with disapproval the use of section 144 for anything Of the nature of a permanent expedient. It is idle to suggest that the Legislature intended section 144, and then if he states his intention of again doing the same thing, a further order may be made against him. The logical conclusion to such a suggestion would be that if a Magistrate chores to allow one day elapsing between the expiry of one order and the issue of another, he is at liberty to continue ad libitum to extend an injunction under section 144 without the sanction of the Local Government." 

 14. A Division Bench of the Calcutta High Court in the of Ashutosh Roy and others Vs. Harish Chandra Chattopadyha (1925) 26 Cr.L.J. 874 held that to draw up order practically in the terms in which a previous order had been passed merely adding to the number of the parties affected amounted to an attempt to evade the provisions of clause (6) of section 144 and could not be regarded as a separate order which could remain inforce for a further period of two months from its date. 

 15. A single Judge of Patna High Court in the case of Ram Narain Vs. Parmesher Prasad, A.IR. 1942 Pat'414 followed 11 C.W.N. 79 and A.I.R. 1917 Pat 154 in holding that a Magistrate had no jurisdiction, to make an order for the renewal of the original order. The case reported as Taturam Sahu Vs. The State of Orissa reported in A.I.R. 1953 Orissa 96 arose out of an order under section 144. Cr.P.C. passed by a Sub-Divisional Magistrate whereby the general public of a certain thane, excepting one particular individual, were restrained from purchasing or exporting Kendu leaves from the said thane. The promulgation of the prohibitory order was alleged to be necessitated by a conflict between two rival groups on a question of property right Ray C.J. in course of a separate order observed that repeated orders in favour of one of the several belligerent parties having conflicting claims to a particular right or property would be beyond the scope and object of the section, and hence improper. 

 "There can be instances where a second order passed after a few days may not be treated to be in continuation of the first, and the second order would be an independent order promulgated under sec. 144. Cr.P.C. For example consider a case where as a result of the order passed under section 144. Cr.P.C. conditions became peaceful and the relations between the rival parties become normal as before the dispute, but all of a sudden after a few days relations between the parties become tense and it is again pretended that a disturbance of public tranquility may take place. In such cases the Magistrate would be acting in good faith when he issues a fresh order under section 144 Cr.P.C. But if conditions do not become peaceful and apprehension is expected even after the expiry of the prescribed period of two months from the date of the issue of the original order under section 144 Cr.P.C. any fresh order to be promulgated under this section would be in continuation of the first and in the eye of law the Magistrate shall be deemed to be promulgating an order for a period exceeding two months an order which would he beyond his jurisdiction. It is a settled law that one cannot do an act indirectly which he could not do directly or that one cannot flout the express provisions of an enactment." 

 18. Learned Deputy Attorney-General, in answer to the aforesaid contention as to the invalidity of a successive. order under section 144 has cited the case of Abdul Himid Qadir Vs. District Magistrate, Lahore, PLD 1957 Lahore 213 and also two cases from the Indian Jurisdiction, namely Babulal Parate Vs. The State of Maharashtra and another, A.I.R. 1961 S.C. 884 and Madhu Limaye Vs Sub-Divisional Magistrate Monghyr, AIR 1971 S.C. 2486. None of these decisions dealt with the case of a successive order, but it has been contended that the said cases have given a lucid exposition is to the scope and ambit of section 144 C.P.C. 

 19. In the Lahore case the validity of an order under section 144 prohibiting any assembly of five or more persons or any procession or demonstration for two months within the limit of Lahore Cantonment came up for consideration. It was alleged that the order had been made in view of a tense situation then prevailing amongst the rival parties of the Lahore Cantonment who were bent upon holding meeting apolitical nature on the, same day and at about the same time near each other. 

 21. In the two Indian Supreme Court cases referred to above, the constitutionality of section 144 of the Code of Criminal Procedure itself was under challenge and in both these cases, the Supreme Court of India generally held the said section to he not violative of any constitutional provision. 

 22. Analysis of all those cases noticed above will show that in most of these cases the making of successive orders under section 144 Cr.P.C. was deprecated and such orders were hell to be unjustified and liable to be set aside; and in those cases where the same orders were practically repeated or the second order was calculated to evade the effect of clause (6) of the section, such orders were declared to have been made without jurisdiction. 

 23. It cannot be disputed that section 144 Cr.P.C. is a temporary expedient and clause (6) has specifically laid down that no order passed under section 144 (1) shall remain in force for more then two months and that it is only the Govt which can extend the operation of such an order. It is clear therefore, that the Magistrate cannot pass an order which has the effect of extending the period of operation of such an order beyond two months and the order which purports to or may be deemed to extend such operation should undoubtedly be regarded as being made without jurisdiction. 

 24. An examination of the relevant provisions of the Code of Criminal Procedure will bear this out. Section 144 constitutes the solitary provision of Chapter XI of the Code which is entitled "Temporary orders in urgent cases of nuisances or apprehended danger". Chapters VIII to XIII are included within Part IV of the Code which is concerned with, as it appears from the title. "Prevention of offences" Chapter VIII which comprises provisions regarding security for keeping the peace and for good behaviour has three divisions. In division A there is section 106 which provides for requiring security for keeping the peace on conviction In division be there are sections 107 to 119 which provide for enforcement of security for keeping the peace in ease of apprehended breach of the peace or disturbance of public tranquility and for keeping the good behavior, from persons disseminating seditious matters, and also from vagrants, suspected persons and habitual offenders and in division C, there are sections 120 to 126A which contain provisions relating to proceedings in the aforesaid cases subsequent to the passing of orders for furnishing security. 

 25. Chanter IX consisting of sections 127 to 132 deals with unravel assemblies and Chapter X provides for prevention of public nuisance, Chapter XII comprising sections 145 to 148 provides for prevention of breach of the peace arising out of disputes relating to immovable property and Chapter XIII consisting of section 149 to 153 deals with the action of the Police for preventing the commission of any cognizable offence. It is thus seen that elaborate provisions have been made in Part IV of the Code for prevention of the commission of certain offences. Chapter XI which comprises section 144 has made provision for making temporary orders in urgent cases of obstruction, annoyance or injury to any person or danger to human life or health, disturbance of public tranquility, riot or affray. 

 26. The first portion of the operative part of sub section (1) of section 144 provides for prevention of nuisance and the second portion provides for prevention of danger to human life health or disturbance of the public tranquility, riot or affray. 

 And whereas a drive has been launched against anti-social elements: And whereas I am satisfied that there is apprehension of breach of the peace and public tranquility while carrying out the drive and that peace cannot be maintained without promulgation of an order under section 144 Cr. P.C. . 

 I) Md. Zahurul Islam, Addl. District Magistrate, Dacca, therefore, in exercise of the powers conferred. on me under section 144 of Criminal Procedure Code, order that no person or presets shall bold in any public place any meeting, rally processions or demonstrations within the jurisdiction of the aforementioned police stations and prohibit assembly of 5 or more persons and the carrying of any weapon of offence. 

 And whereas I am satisfied that there is apprehension of breach of the peace and public tranquility while carrying out the drive and that peace cannot be maintained without promulgation of an order under section 144 Cr P.C. 

 I) Md. Zahurul Islam, Addl. District Magistrate, Dacca therefore, in exercise of the powers conferred on me under section 144 of Criminal Procedure Code order that no persons or persons shall hold in any public place any meeting rally, processions or demonstration within the jurisdiction of the aforementioned police stations and prohibits assembly of 5 or more persona and the carrying of any weapon of offence" 

 "8.... fact is that the life of the order dated 26-4-74 expired on 24-6-74, Thereafter the law and order situation was evaluated by the law enforcing agencies in the light of the happenings of the recent past and various reports and experience of the Additional District Magistrate and he having been satisfied that there was apprehension of breach of the peace and pubic tranquility while carrying out the combined operation for collection of unauthorized arms and against anti-social elements, issued an order ore 25-6-74 under section 144 of the Code of Criminal Procedure......" 

 "13.... The Additional District Magistrate having been satisfied that there were condition prevalent in and around Dacca, on the basis of reports and other materials he passed the order on 25-6-74 imposing restrictions under section 144 of the Code of criminal Procedure to take effect from 6 AM of 26-6-74. The Additional District Magistrate thought it correct that he should give some time so that the people mass notice of the order through publicity media. The restrictions imposts under the said order do not violate any of the provisions of Fundamental Rights guaranteed under the Constitution." 

 38. The preponderant judicial view as has been expressed in the decisions which have been referred to above, is that an order can be made under section 144 Cr.P.C. in case of an emergency for preventing an apprehended danger as to breach of the peace or public tranquility, that the said order can in no event remain in force for more than two months, and that the same order cannot be repeated for preventing the same apprehended danger on the view that the situation has not improved and the danger is still continuing. We are in respectful agreement with the aforesaid view. In a case where there has been no lessening of the danger the clear duty of the persons in charge of the maintenance of public order in the country is, in our opinion, to take recourse to other preventive measures as have been provided in various provisions of the Code of Criminal Procedure, such as sections 107 and 108 of the Code, and not to repeat the order under section 144. We are there fore definitely of the view that the second order under section 144 being nothing but and extension of the first order, the validity of such an order cannot be sustained. 

 39. The next point urged on behalf of the petitioner is that the impugned order cannot be regarded as a valid order under section 144 inasmuch as it is not in conformity to the terms of that section. The learned Advocate for the petitioner has submitted that it is essential, as is apparent from the provisions of the section, that the material facts from which the Magistrate had been satisfied that for prevention of certain obstruction, injury or danger to lire or disturbance of public tranquility or peace, the exercise of the emergency power under the said section had become a necessity, should have been set out in the order. The Magistrate in exercising this power is to act judicially and it appears from the recitals in the order that there is no causal relationship between the facts stated in the order and the apprehended danger, it cannot but is considered to be colorable exercise of the power granted under the said provision. The learned Advocate for the petitioner in support of his contention has relied upon a Full Bench decision of the Lahore High Court in the case of P.T. Chandra, Editor, Tribune Vs. Emperor, A.I.R. 1942 Lahore. 171. In that case, an order under section 144 Cr. P.C, whereby publication of any article concerning a Hartal against the Sales Tax or concerning Police action taken against the processionists or persons otherwise assisting or taking part in the Fatal, in any newspaper or pamphlet within Lahore District was prohibited, had been challenged Chief Justice Yong in delivering the lea dine judgment of the Full Bench expressed himself in the following manner: 

 "In this order no material facts, which would justify the order, have been given. To justify an order under section 144 there must be a causal connection between the act prohibited and the danger apprehended to prevent which the order is passed. It is not stated in the order nor is it alleged, that the publication of news about the Hartal had led in the past to the formation of unlawful processions. Nor has any connection been shown between the articles to he published in the Press and the alleged danger of disturbance of public tranquility," 

 40. In the present case also in the impugned order no facts other than preparation for holding meetings rallies and demonstrations in the City and launching of combined operation for collecting unauthorized arms and against antisocial elements have been mentioned No causal relation between these two items of facts have been shown or indicated. No further facts have been disclosed in the affidavit opposition filed on behalf of the respondents nor any serious attempt has been made to show how the prohibited acts, namely, holding of meeting, processions rallies or demonstrations might have had any effect on the combined operation. It does not suffice merely to recite certain facts in the order without showing the causal relationship between the said facts and the apprehended danger. It is now well established that a Magistrate functioning under section 144 is to act judicially and as he is required to state the material facts of the case in the order made under the said section, some kind of nexus between the prohibited acts and in apprehended danger should be indicated. It has nowhere been disclosed how the holding of a public Ideating or taking cut a procession in a peaceful manner might adversely affect the success of the combined operation nor it has been suggested that the objective of the public meetings, rallies and demonstrations referred to in the impugned order was hostile to or obstructive of the said operation. No materials have been placed before us to show that a law and order situation is likely to be created on a comparatively wide scale because of the holding of such public meeting rallies or demonstrations leading to disturbance of public order, so that it can be suggested that such meetings, rallies or demonstrations require to be prohibited in the interests of public order. Went therefore, are of opinion that no causal relationship having been shown to exist between the facts stated in the order and the apprehended danger, this order cannot be regarded to be a valid order within the meaning of section 144 Cr.P.C. 

 41. This question may also be tested from the standpoint of the constitutional guarantees. The constitutional point involved in this case is two fold; firstly, whether section 144 Cr.P.C. which was an existing law at the commencement of the constitution and under which the impugned order has been made is inconsistent with Art, 33 within the meaning of Art, 26 (1) of the Constitution arid secondly. Whether, in case of section 144 Cr.P.C. being held to be constitutional the impugned order itself is violative of Art, 37 and as such was beyond the scope of section 144 Cr.P.C. 

 42. The impugned order is directed against the holding of any public meeting, demonstration, rally or procession of assembly of 5 or more persons in the City of Dacca and Narayanganj until further orders. Article 37, unlike the analogous provision in the Indian Constitution or Pakistan Constitutions of 1956 or 1962 which were previously in force in this territory now Bangladesh, declares specifically a citizen's fundamental right to participate in public winnings and processions, in addition to his general right to assemble. These rights can no don’t the curtailed or regulated by a law imposing reasonable restrictions in the interests not public order or public health. It will therefore be necessary to examine the restrictions as have been prescribed under section 144 Cr.P.C. and also those as have been enforced by the impugned order, for the purpose of determine the whether they are reasonable in the interest of public order. It is nobody's case that these restrictions imposed by the impugned order had to do anything with public health. 

 44. Section 144 of the Code of Criminal Procedure empowers the District or local authority, representing the executive organ of the State, to make prohibitory orders having the effect of restricting the exercise of a fundamental right in an emergency as an temporary measure for preventing certain nuisance, danger to human life or health, the disturbance of the public tranquility; a riot or an affray. In Order to decide the constitutionality of this provision we are to consider first whether the object of making an order under the said provision, as has been stated therein, can be regarded to be in the interests of public order. 

 46. This question again came up for consideration in the case of Madhu Limaye Vs. Sub Divisional Magistrate, Monghyr A.I.R 1971 (S.C.) 2486 in Which the constitutionality of section 144 Cr. P. Code was re-examined, although its constitutionality was previously upheld in the case of Bahulal Parate Vs. The State of Maharashtra A.I.R 1961 (S. C.) 884, as the Supreme Court of India, while laying down its opinion in the latter case; examined the question with reference to reasonable restrictions for the maintenance of law and order, and not 'in the interests of public order' which is the precise language of the constitutional provision. Chief Justice Hedayetullah who delivered the judgment of the Court in Madhu Limay's case gave a wider meaning to the expression 'public order' in the said case than what he himself gave to the said expression in Ram Monohar Lohia' case (AIR. 1966 (S.C) 740) 'in connection with the interpretation of the phrase 'maintenance of public order' as used in rule 30 (1)(b) of Defence of India Rules, 1962, and expressed himself in the following manner : 

 47. The objective of an action under section 144 as expressed in the section itself is the prevention of a nuisance or a certain harmful, occurrence, danger to human life or health, disturbance of the public tranquility or a riot or an affray Under Art 37 or the Constitution, imposition of certain restrictions upon the fundamental rights declared in the said Article, which are to be reasonable in the interests of public order or public health, is permissible Leaving out the matter relating to public health, with which we are not concerned in this case, the restrictions contemplated in section 144 must conform to the standard of reasonableness declared in Article 37 of which the guide line is the interests of public order. We have already noticed that the expression 'in the interests of public order' is not to be understood in the restricted sense. The expression 'in the interests of public order' is undoubtedly Wider than the maintenance of public order but such a power can be exercised only in urgent cases, of apprehended danger and the order which must necessarily be of temporary duration can not, in view of sub-section (6), remain in force for more than two months. It is true that in cases of emergency and in certain other cases the order may be promulgated exporter but the Magistrate shall have to set out the material facts and the order which is to and served in the prescribed manner. Furthermore, in sub-sections (4) and (5) provisions have been made for rescission or alteration of the order by the Magistrate passing the order suo motu or an application by an aggrieved person. 

 48. The maximum period of two months for which a peremptory order by a Magistrate under section 144 Cr.P.C may remain in force may be considered to be a reasonable limit. The legislative intent is clear that it is not for him to extend the period of operation of such an order, even if there has been no improvement in the station Under the second part of subsection (6) it n the Government which is empowered to expedite period of operation. It may he mended, however, that the Supreme Court of India has declared this part in the sub-section to be unconstitutional in the case of The State of Bihar Vs K. K. Mishara, A.I.R. 1971. S.C. 1667 we are however, not concerned with the question of constitutionality of this part in the instant case. 

 49. The Supreme Court of In has generally upheld the constitutionality of section 144 Cr.P.C in the two cases referred to above, namely Babulal Parate Vs. The State of Maharastra, AIR, 1961 S.C. 884 and 1Vfadhu Limaye Vs. The Sub-Divisional Magistrate Monghyr AIR 1971 SC 2486 Chief Justice Hidayatullah in laying down the of the Supreme Court of India in this regard, in Madhu Limaye's case in which Babutal Parate's ease was also reconsidered, made the following observation: 

 "The gist of action under section 144 is the urgency of the isolation, its efficacy in the likelihood of being able to prevent some harmful occurrence, As it is possible to act absolutely and even expert, it is obvious that the emergency must be sudden and the con sequences sufficiently grave. Without it the exercise of power would have no rustication. It is not an ordinary power flowing from administration but a power used in a judicial manner and which can stand further judicial scrutiny in the been for the exercise of the power, in its efficacy and in the extent of its application. There is no general proposition that an order under section 144 Criminal Procedure Code cannot be passed without taking evidence.” 

 50. We find ourselves in respectful agreement with the view taken in the said case by the Supreme Court of India. Having regard to the fact that the object of prevention of the apprehended danger to human life, disturbance of the public tranquility riot or an affray is closely allied to the interests of public order, we are of option that the restriction on the individual right is contemplated in the second portion of the operative pert of section 144(1) cannot be said to be unreasonable and as such the aforesaid provision of the Code cannot be held to be unconstitutional. 

 58. It may sometimes happen that certain persons may organize public meetings or demonstrations not so much in exercise of their democratic right, as with an ulterior purpose of subverting public order or May also happen that meetings and demonstrations with perfectly lawful purposes may lead to problems effecting law and order on a large scale, because of action some other groups having different purposes. A grave situation likely to result in disruption of law and order may suddenly arise. The provisions section 144 can certainly be invoked to Meet such a situation when any other preventive action is not feasible eases of emergency this power cause no doubt, be exercised ex parte without nay opportunity being afforded to the person against Whom it is sought to be made. 

 whether there is necessity for the excrcise of this power in the interests of public order or whether there is emergency within the meaning of sub-section (2) is indipulably within the jurisdiction of the Magistrate concerned. But as Chief Justice Hidayatullah of Indian Supreme Court observed in Madhu Limaye's case, AIR 1971 (S.C) 2486 at page 2496, the power a the exercised under section 144. Cr. P.C is not an ordinary power flowing froth  administration but a power used in a judicial manner and which cap stand further judicial scrutiny in the need for the exercise of the power, in its efficacy And in the extent of its application. The Magistrate charged with the duty of exercising such power is therefore required to state the material facts on the basis which the necessary formation of the opinion has been made, and is for the Court to see whether the preventive action curbing the fundamental right is reasonable in the interest of the public order.
